title: One-shot contrast studio
content:
Purpose: quick playground for one-shot contrast prompts. Notes to self, rough sketches, observed brittle cases and fast mitigation ideas. Keep small, iterate, and pick a few variants for formal eval later.

Context / motivation:
- Many downstream tasks prefer tiny prompts (1-shot) to reduce token cost and simplify template management.
- But 1-shot can wildly change when exemplar phrasing/ordering shifts. Want a catalog of robust contrastive examples and lightweight heuristics to make one-shot behave more like small few-shot ensembles.

Experiment structure (ad-hoc):
- Task families: classification (binary/multi), short freeform generation, instruction-following (formatting), extraction (entity lists).
- For each task: 4 exemplar variants (neutral, negative-anchored, positive-anchored, minimal exemplar).
- Metrics: top-line accuracy/ROUGE on small eval set, and two qualitative checks: hallucination sign, format adherence.

Quick checklist before running:
- seed examples saved as triple: (prompt_template, exemplar_text, expected_output_trim)
- randomized order runs to catch ordering sensitivity
- log model+temp+max_tokens+stop sequences

Sketch prompts: (use as-is for quick manual tests)
1) Binary sentiment (movie review)
- Template A (neutral exemplar):
  You are a sentiment analyzer. Classify the sentiment of the following review as POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.
  Example: "The movie kept me awake with excitement and heart — I loved it. -> POSITIVE"
  Review: "{review}" ->
- Variant notes: neutral exemplar uses emotive language. Test with very short reviews and with sarcasm.

2) Extract tech stack from job description
- Template B (negative-anchored exemplar):
  Extract all programming languages and frameworks mentioned. If none, reply NONE.
  Example: "Experience with C++ and Qt, plus Python scripting. -> C++; Qt; Python"
  Job: "{job_text}" ->
- Variant notes: negative-anchored = exemplar deliberately lists items separated by semicolons. Check whether model obeys delimiter.

3) Formatting: markdown bullets from bulletless paragraph
- Template C (minimal exemplar):
  Convert the paragraph below into a concise markdown bullet list (3–5 bullets).
  Example: "We improved load time. We also shipped analytics. -> - improved load time
- shipped analytics"
  Paragraph: "{para}" ->
- Variant notes: minimal exemplar shows short mapping. Test with noisy punctuation.

Observed brittle failure modes (from quick manual probes):
- Exemplar-anchoring overfitting: When the exemplar uses explicit punctuation style (comma vs semicolon) the model often mirrors that exactly even if the input suggests a different delimiter. Means exemplar can bias surface form decisions.
- Label leakage in instruction: including the arrow "->" in the exemplar increases chance of producing the label in an unexpected context (e.g., appending "-> NEGATIVE" in longer outputs).
- Sarcasm flip: single-sentence sarcastic reviews often misclassified; adding a short clarifier in the exemplar (e.g., "clearly sarcastic") reduces but introduces heuristic leakage.

Quick candidate mitigations to test next: (prioritized)
1) Neutralize exemplar surface form: use generic phrasing like "Label:" instead of punctuation arrows.
2) Provide one-line rubric instead of exemplar for sensitive tasks (e.g., "If sentiment unclear, pick NEGATIVE for safety").
3) Use a micro-ensemble: run 3 exemplars (different styles) at temp=0 and majority vote. Compare token cost vs accuracy lift.
4) Controlled delimiter instruction: append "Return items separated by semicolon" explicitly for extraction tasks (counteracts exemplar bias).

Tiny experiments run log (manual, noisy):
- 2025-11-10: Binary sentiment quick run, 10 examples, model-x/1.2, temp=0.5, exemplar with arrow: accuracy 0.6, many outputs included arrow text verbatim.
- 2025-11-17: Swap exemplar to "Label:" style: accuracy 0.72, fewer verbatim artifacts but slightly longer tokens.
- 2025-12-02: Extract tech stack, added delimiter instruction: precision improved for multi-language lines but recall dipped when frameworks embedded in sentences.

Failure case catalog (short examples to reproduce):
- Input (sentiment): "Oh great, another two hours of nonstop excitement." Expected: NEGATIVE (sarcasm) -> Model: POSITIVE at temp>0.3
- Input (extraction): "We use Python for infra, SQL for warehouse, and sometimes R for analytics" -> Model sometimes misses R when exemplar lists only 2 items.

Notes on one-shot exemplar design patterns (hypotheses):
- Anchoring strength correlates with exemplar lexical overlap: if exemplar shares uncommon tokens with target, bias increases. So pick exemplars with neutral vocabulary.
- Surface-form priming stronger than semantic priming for short prompts — punctuation and delimiters matter more than paraphrase content.
- Rubric + minimal exemplar seems to give good tradeoff for extraction tasks.

Small checklist for converting winners into canonical mini-templates:
- replace unique named entities with placeholders (\{ORG\}, \{LANG\})
- avoid arrows and literal tokens that might get copied into responses
- include an explicit output schema line (e.g., "Return items separated by semicolon, no extra commentary")
- add 1–2 negative examples only for tasks where false positives are costly

Potential next experiments (2–4 week plan):
- Systematic sweep: for 50-shot subsample evaluate 20 one-shot exemplar variants per task family, log delta vs a 5-shot baseline.
- Micro-ensemble ablation: varying exemplar diversity vs cost per call.
- Low-temp vs 0 temp: how stochasticity interacts with exemplar anchoring.
- Evaluation harness: automated small bench (50 items each) with deterministic seeds, store outputs in repo linked above.

Loose implementation notes (for when we formalize):
- store exemplar templates in CSV: columns = task, exemplar_id, exemplar_text, surface_style_tag, rubric_line
- runner picks N exemplars by surface_style_tag diversity and runs in parallel where possible

Todo (short):
- [ ] formalize 10 canonical templates for eng use-cases (sentiment, extraction, summarization, formatting, code-brief)
- [ ] hook up small bench in repo (create script and PR)
- [ ] schedule 1hr sync with Ethan and Maya to triage failure cases and pick next priorities

Random scribbles / heuristics to remember:
- When in doubt, ask for an explicit "schema line" to force format.
- Prefer semicolons for list extraction (less ambiguous in free text).
- Use neutral lexicon in exemplar to reduce topical anchoring.

End of file.

(If I revisit, consider renaming to 'one-shot-contrast-lab' when we formalize.)
